name: Amazon Timestream
license: Proprietary service; Timestream for InfluxDB runs open-source InfluxDB 2.x (MIT) and InfluxDB 3 Core (MIT or Apache 2.0), while InfluxDB 3 Enterprise and 2.x read replicas add InfluxData licence fees
summary: AWS’s time-series databases: a serverless engine now closed to new customers, and managed InfluxDB 2 and 3.
intro: The name covers two different products. Timestream for LiveAnalytics, generally available since September 2020, is serverless: you create databases and tables and send records (a timestamp, dimensions such as `well_id`, and measures) through the AWS SDK. Writes land in an in-memory store replicated across three Availability Zones; after a retention period you set per table, data moves to a magnetic store laid out for large reads, and late-arriving data can be written there directly. Tables split into partitions by time and by dimension values, and SQL queries with time-series functions run on a worker fleet sized to each query, billed in Timestream Compute Units (one TCU is 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory). AWS closed LiveAnalytics to new customers on June 20, 2025; existing accounts keep using it, and AWS points newcomers to Timestream for InfluxDB.

Timestream for InfluxDB, generally available since March 2024, is managed InfluxDB priced like a database server: you pick an instance class and storage, and AWS runs the open-source engine in your VPC with patching, backups and optional Multi-AZ failover. It started with InfluxDB 2.7; read replica clusters need an InfluxData add-on bought in AWS Marketplace. Since October 2025 it also runs InfluxDB 3 as clusters that keep data as Parquet files in Amazon S3 and cache recent data on the nodes. The Core edition is one node without compaction, meant for recent data; Enterprise grows to 15 nodes (since March 2026), compacts files for long retention, and adds an InfluxData licence fee per vCPU-hour. In US East (N. Virginia) on 2026-10-06, a `db.influx.large` instance cost $0.239 an hour, LiveAnalytics queries $0.518 per TCU-hour, and InfluxDB 3 storage $0.023 per GB-month.
strengths: Existing LiveAnalytics users get a database with no servers to size or patch, where ingestion, storage and queries scale separately and data tiers from memory to magnetic storage on its own
Timestream for InfluxDB keeps the open InfluxDB APIs, line protocol, Telegraf and client libraries, so code moves between self-hosted InfluxDB and AWS
InfluxDB 3 clusters keep data in S3 and bill storage on what is actually stored, separately from compute
AWS operations built in: Multi-AZ standby with automatic failover, backups and restore, maintenance windows, customer managed KMS keys, VPC and IAM integration
limits: LiveAnalytics is closed to new customers since June 20, 2025; AWS’s migration guide exports data to S3 and loads it into Timestream for InfluxDB or Aurora/RDS PostgreSQL
Timestream for InfluxDB is not serverless: instances bill every hour they run (per second, 10-minute minimum), and Multi-AZ doubles both instance and storage prices
Licence fees on top of AWS charges: 2.x read replicas and InfluxDB 3 Enterprise are billed by InfluxData through AWS Marketplace, and the read replica add-on can only be subscribed to in the console
InfluxDB 3 Core is a single node without compaction that AWS doesn’t recommend for long-term storage, and every InfluxDB 3 cluster pays for at least 200 GB of storage
No host access, and InfluxDB 2.x instances top out at 16 TiB of storage; AWS advises staying under 10 million series per instance

story: AWS announced Amazon Timestream at re:Invent in November 2018 as a preview of a serverless time-series database for server logs, sensor data and industrial telemetry. Its pitch was cost and scale: AWS claimed it would process trillions of events a day at one tenth the cost of relational databases, keeping recent data in memory and moving history to cheaper storage automatically.

General availability took nearly two years, until September 2020. Scheduled queries, multi-measure records and direct writes to the magnetic store followed in 2021, and compute-unit query pricing in 2024. Meanwhile many teams already ran InfluxDB, so in March 2024 AWS added a second engine under the same name: managed open-source InfluxDB, in the style of RDS.

In May 2025 AWS said it would close the original engine, renamed Timestream for LiveAnalytics, to new customers from June 20, 2025, and recommended InfluxDB instead. Managed InfluxDB 3, with data on S3, arrived in October 2025.

choices.choice: Serverless, with ingestion, storage and queries decoupled
choices.why: AWS wanted each layer to scale on its own and to avoid correlated failures as the system grows, so customers never size servers.

choices.choice: A memory store and a magnetic store in one table
choices.why: Most time-series writes and dashboard reads touch recent data, so it stays in memory, while older data moves to storage organized for large scans, and one query reads across both.

choices.choice: Partitions split by dimension values as well as time
choices.why: Nearly all writes arrive around the current time, so splitting by time alone would not spread write traffic or let queries skip data.

choices.choice: Run open-source InfluxDB for the second engine
choices.why: Teams with InfluxDB code, Telegraf agents and dashboards could move to a managed service without rewriting against a new API.

timeline.text: Timestream announced in preview at re:Invent
Generally available in September in four Regions
